                                                                    GENERAL SYMMETRIC IDEALS

                                                                   ALEXANDRA SECELEANU AND LIANA ŞEGA


                                                   Abstract. We investigate the structure and properties of symmetric ideals gener-
                                                   ated by general forms in the polynomial ring under the natural action of the sym-




arXiv:2506.15459v1 [math.AC] 18 Jun 2025
                                                   metric group. This work significantly broadens the framework established in our
                                                   earlier collaboration with Harada on principal symmetric ideals [15]. A novel aspect
                                                   of our approach is the construction of a bijective parametrization of general sym-
                                                   metric ideals using Macaulay-Matlis duality, which is asymptotically independent of
                                                   the number of variables of the ambient ring. We establish that general symmetric
                                                   ideals exhibit extremal behavior in terms of Hilbert functions and Betti numbers,
                                                   and satisfy the Weak Lefschetz Property. We also demonstrate explicit asymptotic
                                                   stability in their algebraic and homological invariants under increasing numbers of
                                                   variables, showing that such ideals form well-behaved S∞ –invariant chains.

                                                                                  1. Introduction
                                             Let k be a field and let R = k[x1 , . . . , xn ] denote the polynomial ring in n variables.
                                           Let I be a homogeneous ideal in R, i.e., an ideal generated by homogeneous polyno-
                                           mials f1 , . . . , fr of degrees d1 , . . . , dr , respectively. A theme of investigation with a
                                           few decades of tradition in commutative algebra concerns the properties of the cyclic
                                           module R/I as the polynomials f1 , . . . , fr are chosen to be as independent as possible.
                                           For example, if r ≤ n this means that f1 , . . . , fr form a regular sequence and thus R/I

                                              Date: June 19, 2025.
                                              2010 Mathematics Subject Classification. Primary: 13D02. Secondary 13A50, 13F20.
                                              Key words and phrases. General symmetric ideal, Betti numbers, asymptotic stability, Weak Lef-
                                           schetz Property.
                                                                                            1
2                                    A. SECELEANU AND L. ŞEGA

is a complete intersection, while for r ≥ n the ring R/I is a finite dimensional k-vector
space, thus an artinian k-algebra.
     It was shown by Fröberg and Löfwall in [12] that, for fixed values of n, d1 , . . . , dr ,
there exists only a finite number of possible Hilbert series for R/I. Moreover, there
is a Zariski open subset in the space of coefficients of the fi ’s on which the Hilbert
series of R/I is the same and it is in fact the minimal series among all possible Hilbert
series of quotients with the same parameters. Famously, a longstanding conjecture by
Fröberg describes this minimal Hilbert series [10] and is related to Lefschetz properties
of artinian rings. One calls algebras with this Hilbert series general. In complete
generality Fröberg’s conjecture has proven elusive, however the following works make
partial progress: [10] (n = 2), [2] (n=3), [34] (r = n + 1), [31] (infinitely many cases
with d1 = d2 = · · · = dr ).
     There is an additional conjecture due to Migliore and Miró-Roig [24, Conjecture 5.8]
regarding the betti numbers of general algebras R/I with I equigenerated (d1 = d2 =
· · · = dr ). It asserts that such algebras would possess minimal Betti numbers consistent
with the Fröberg Hilbert function. A number of particular cases are elucidated in [24].
     Another method to specify an ideal I defining an artinian quotient R/I is by means
of its Macaulay inverse system I −1 (see (2.1)). Macaulay-Matlis duality relates the
R-modules R/I and I −1 to each other. Iarrobino defines compressed algebras as a
class of graded algebras parametrized by their Macaulay inverse systems that exhibit
extremal behavior in their Hilbert function. Specifically, compressed algebras have the
maximal Hilbert function possible given the dimension of their socle and the embedding
dimension. These rings are studied in [18, 17, 11, 14], among others. With respect to the
parametrization corresponding to the inverse system compressed algebras are general,
meaning that they form a dense Zariski open set. In [5] Boij studies the betti numbers
of compressed level algebras giving lower bounds for these numbers and finding that
these lower bounds are attained by compressed algebras of large enough socle degree.
This leaves open several questions which are still being investigated. In [33] Rossi and
Şega study resolutions of modules over compressed Gorenstein local rings showing that
all such modules have rational Poincaré series with a common denominator.
     Inspired by these well-known problems and results, our goal in this paper is to
discuss analogous phenomena concerning graded algebras equipped with an action of
the symmetric group. To construct such algebras, consider the natural action of the
symmetric group Sn on the polynomial ring R = k[x1 , . . . , xn ] given by

                  σ · f (x1 , . . . , xn ) = f (xσ(1) , . . . , xσ(n) )   for σ ∈ Sn .

We are interested in homogeneous ideals which acquire an induced action from the
action of Sn on R, which we refer to as symmetric ideals. The study of such ideals
is both a classical topic in commutative algebra and one of current interest. In par-
ticular, the graded betti numbers for (certain families of) monomial symmetric ideals
are the focus of the recent works [13], [25], [4] and [26] and related invariants such
as Castelnuovo-Mumford regularity are studied in [32, 23]. The symmetric ideals dis-
cussed in this paper behave quite differently from most symmetric monomial ideals and
therefore novel methods are introduced to study them in our work. We were inspired
to study general symmetric ideals by [21], which describes the radical of such an ideal.
                              GENERAL SYMMETRIC IDEALS                                   3

   In this paper, we focus initially on homogeneous symmetric ideals having all minimal
generators of the same degree, deducing later that this is not a restrictive assumption
(see Remark 7.13). We term (r, d)-symmetric ideals those symmetric ideals that can
be generated up to the action of the symmetric group by an r-dimensional vector
space of homogeneous polynomials of degree d. Such ideals can be parametrized          by
                                                                    n+d−1
                                                                           
the Grassmannian variety of r-dimensional subspaces of the N =         d     -dimensional
vector space of forms of degree d forms, Rd . This parametrization is given by a map Φ
that takes a vector space V to the ideal (V )Sn generated by the orbits of elements of
V under the action of the symmetric group Sn . To summarize, we have an onto map:
             Φ : Gr(r, Rd ) → (r, d)-symmetric ideals                                (1.1)
             Φ(V ) := (V )Sn ,       where (V )Sn = (σ · f : σ ∈ Sn , f ∈ V ).
The case r = 1 has been considered in our previous work [15] joint with M. Harada,
where the (1, d)-symmetric ideals are called principal symmetric ideals.
   Another way to parametrize symmetric ideals stems from Macaulay duality. The
inverse system of a symmetric ideal of R is an R-submodule of a dual ring S (see 2.1).
This ring is also equipped with an action of Sn . In [15] we discovered that the inverse
system of a principal symmetric ideal is generated by Sn -invariant polynomials in S.
Therefore we consider the rings of invariant polynomials R′ = PRSn and S ′ = S Sn . Their
                                                             1
elements form the image of the Reynolds operator ρ(f ) = n! σ∈Sn σ · f applied to R
and S respectively. A key component of our approach is to parametrize the symmetric
ideals of R that have inverse systems generated by elements of S ′ . Specifically we term
a quotient R/I a narrow algebra with (s, d)–invariant socle if the inverse system has
the form I −1 = W + S≥−d+1 , where W is a vector subspace of S−d     ′  and dimk (W ) = s.
                    ′        ′
   Working with R and S presents the advantage that up to isomorphism the graded
vector spaces Rd′ and S−d ′    only depend on d and not on n, provided that n ≥ d. This
allows to parametrize narrow algebra having (s, d)–invariant socle by a significantly
smaller space than the source of (1.1) above, which has the advantage of being uniform,
that is, independent of the number of variables and dependent only upon s and d. To
set this up, consider the following map induced by ρ
                                   [
               α : Gr(r, Rd ) →        Gr(i, Rd′ ) α(V ) := ⟨ρ(f ) : f ∈ V ⟩.        (1.2)
                                 0≤i≤r

Moreover we denote by β the map
                                          ′
                       β : Gr(P (d) − r, S−d ) → symmetric ideals                    (1.3)
                       β(W ) := AnnR (W + S≥−d+1 ),
where the operator AnnR (−) implements Macaulay-Matlis duality as described in 2.1
and P (d) denotes the number of partitions of d with at most n parts, which is equal to
dimk Rd′ and also dimk S−d
                         ′ .

   Assuming that n is sufficiently large, in the course our investigation we find nonempty
Zariski open sets O ⊂ Gr(r, Rd ) and G ⊂ Gr(r, Rd′ ) so that α(O) = G, and diagram
(1.4) below commutes.
   We call the ideal Φ(V ) = (V )Sn a general (r, d)-symmetric ideal whenever V ∈ O,
see Definition 7.5.

    Denoting the composition of ⊥ and β in (1.4) by Ψ gives an alternate parametrization
                              Ψ : G → (r, d)-symmetric ideals.                            (1.5)
In view of the surjectivity of Ψ, which we establish in Theorem 7.9, every general
symmetric ideal is of the form Ψ(U ) for a unique U ∈ G. This shows that, like Φ,
Ψ is a parametrization of the general (r, d)-symmetric ideals, but it is superior to Φ
because Ψ is one-to-one and the parametrizing space G is independent of the number
of variables, provided n ≥ d.
   Our results regarding diagram (1.4) can be summarized as follows.
Theorem A (Theorem 7.9). Suppose k is infinite with char(k) = 0 or char(k) > n and
let d, r be positive integers with r ≤ P (d). Assume n is sufficiently large. Then there
exist nonempty open sets O ⊆ Gr(r, Rd ) and G ⊆ Gr(r, Rd′ ) such that
    (1) diagram (1.4) commutes,
    (2) Ψ(G) = Φ(O),
    (3) α(O) = G and
    (4) Ψ|G is bijective and thus (1.5) gives a birational parametrization of (r, d)-
         symmetric ideals in terms of the parameter space Gr(r, kP (d) ).
   The parametrization through the map Φ is well suited to establishing algebraic and
homological properties of general (r, d)-symmetric ideals. We summarize them in Theo-
rem B below, noting that item (2) says that general (r, d)-symmetric ideals are extremal
in terms of their Hilbert functions among all symmetric ideals with the same number
of generators up to symmetry, while item (3) presents the betti numbers of such ideals
as being nearly minimal consistent with the Hilbert function in (2) (the minimal such
betti numbers would additionally satisfy ℓ · b = 0).
Theorem B (Theorem 7.10, Corollary 7.11). Suppose k is infinite with char(k) = 0 or
char(k) > n and fix positive integers d, r. Assume

  Moreover, the Poincaré series of all finitely generated graded A-modules are rational,
sharing a common denominator. When d > 2 or d = 1 the ring A is Golod. When
d = 2, then A is Koszul. The ring A is Gorenstein if and only if d = 2 and r = 1, or
d = 1.
   Our previous paper [15] contains similar results in the case when r = 1, that can
be recovered from Theorem B and served as inspiration for our approach. The recent
paper [35] by N. Walker leads to the effective bound on n given in Theorem B and
shows this bound is tight, while independent results presented in this paper establish
the validity of Theorem B for large enough n without providing an explicit value.
   To generalize our previous results, we now let the number of variables of the poly-
nomial ring R grow to infinity. To be more precise, for each positive integer n we let
Rn = k[x1 , . . . , xn ]. The colimit of the rings Rn under their natural inclusions,Swhere n
ranges over the positive integers, admits a natural action of the group S∞ = n≥1 Sn
of permutations of N that have finitely many non-fixed points. This action is of utmost
importance in the study of representation stability for symmetric group representa-
tions. A major achievement in this setting is the development of Noetherianity up to
symmetry for ideals of this (non-Noetherian) colimit and its applications to uniformity
in commutative algebra; see [6], [3], [16], [9], [7].
   If I is a symmetric ideal of Rm for some m, we define a sequence
                              I = Im ⊆ Im+1 ⊆ . . . In ⊆ . . .                         (1.6)
where In is the ideal of Rn for all n ≥ m described by In = (Im )Sn . The chain (1.6) is a
S∞ -invariant chain, meaning that Sn′ (In ) ⊆ In′ for all m ≤ n ≤ n′ . Properties of S∞ -
invariant chains have been studied from the viewpoint of commutative algebra in [29, 22,
23, 32, 26], among many others. A main problem in this area is to study the asymptotic
growth of various numerical invariants for S∞ -invariant chains of homogeneous ideals.
6                                 A. SECELEANU AND L. ŞEGA

   In view of our results, a natural question raised by C. Raicu is whether I being a
general (r, d)-symmetric ideal implies the same is true about the subsequent ideals in
the chain (1.6). While this is far from evident from the perspective of the parametriza-
tion (1.1), we succeed in answering this question in the affirmative by making use of
the alternate parametrization (1.5), particularly its feature that the parameter space
Gr(r, Rd′ ) is independent of the number of variables of R, provided n ≥ d. This leads
to the realization that diagrams of the form (1.4) where the number of variables of R
varies can be made compatible in a manner made precise in Theorem 9.2. This cru-
cial ingredient allows us to analyze the asymptotic behavior of numerical invariants in
chains of general S∞ -invariant ideals, answering [20, Problem 1.1] for chains of general
symmetric ideals.
Theorem C (Theorem 9.2, Theorem 9.3). Suppose k is a field with char(k) = 0 and
let d, r be positive integers with r ≤ P (d). Assume m ≫ 0. Let I be a general (r, d)-
symmetric ideal of Rm , and consider the S∞ -invariant chain {In }n∈N with In = (I)Sn
and its colimit I. For a, ℓ as defined in Theorem B(3) the following hold:
    (1) the ideals In = (Im )Sn are general (r, d)-symmetric ideals for all n ≥ m.
    (2) dim(Rn /In ) = 0 and ht(In ) = n for all n ≥ m, i.e, the rings Rn /In are artinian.
    (3) pdRn (Rn /In ) = n for all n ≥ m
    (4) regRn (R/In ) = d for all n ≥ m
    (5) the i-th betti numbers of Rn /In are polynomials in n of degree d + i for 0 ≤ i ≤
         n − 1, while the n-th betti number of Rn /In is a linear function of n.
    (6) The equivariant Hilbert series (defined in (9.4)) is
                                   hP                 i
                                     d          j td−j + a(1 − s)d−1 td
                                 s   j=0 (1 − s)
                     HI (s, t) =                                        .
                                                (1 − s)d
      (7) The multiplicity of Rn /In grows polynomially as a function of n with
                                      e(Rn /In )      1
                                   lim    d−1
                                                 =          .
                                  n→∞   n          (d − 1)!
       (8) The equivariant betti number βi,j (I, s) (defined in (9.7)) is a rational function
            of s for all i, j, and the equivariant bigraded Poincaré series PI (s, t, u) is a
            rational function of s, t, u. More precisely,
                                                                                         

    PI (s, t, u) =     +stu                         −                     +                  .
                   1−s            (1−s)(1−s−stu)d (1−s−stu)(1−stu)              1 − stu
   Theorem C shows that S∞ -invariant chains of general symmetric ideals are much
better behaved than arbitrary S∞ -invariant chains. For instance, for our chains the
Krull dimension and regularity are constant, while for arbitrary chains the former
exhibits linear growth [29, Theorem 7.10] and the latter is proven in the artinian case
and conjectured in general to grow linearly [23]. Moreover for our chains the multiplicity
grows polynomially as a function of n, while for arbitrary S∞ -invariant chains the
growth is exponential [29, Theorem 7.10].
   Our paper is organized as follows. In Section 2 we recall the technical foundations
of our work: Macaulay-Matlis duality and the notions of narrow and extremely narrow
algebras introduced in [15]. We also prove a new result that the latter class of algebras
                               GENERAL SYMMETRIC IDEALS                                       7

enjoys the Weak Lefschetz Property, an algebraic counterpart of Lefschetz’s hyperplane
section theorem. In Section 3 we discuss a perfect pairing among symmetric polyno-
mials and in Section 4 we use it to study linear syzygies on symmetric polynomials.
In Section 5 we define the open set G in (1.4), show it does not depend on n as long
as n ≥ d, and prove that algebras in Ψ(G) are d-extremely narrow (Theorem 5.2).
Under the additional assumption that n is sufficiently large so as to enable a certain
construction, we determine in Section 6 the generators of a general symmetric ideal.
Turning our attention to the parametrization Φ in (1.1), we show in Section 7 that
the open set O in (1.4) is non-empty and prove Theorem A and Theorem B. Section 8
reveals the surprising fact that if n ≫ 0 and I is a general symmetric ideal then the
inverse system of the ideal I ′ = ρ(I) of R′ determines the inverse system of I. This can
be viewed as a manifestation of the fact that the parametrization Φ factors through α
as indicated in (1.4) and explains why inverse systems of general symmetric ideals are
generated by invariant polynomials. Finally, in Section 9 we turn our attention to S∞
invariant chains of symmetric ideals and prove Theorem C.

                     2. Inverse systems and narrow algebras
   Throughout, k denotes a field, n ≥ 2 an integer and R = k[x1 , . . . , xn ] the polynomial
ring in n variables of degree 1 over k. We denote by m the maximal homogeneous ideal
of R. In this section, we recall the basics of the theory of Macaulay inverse systems.
Then we give an overview of narrow and extremely narrow algebras as introduced in
[15], extend some of the results therein and establish that extremely narrow algebras
satisfy the Weak Lefschetz Property.

2.1. Duality and inverse systems. We give here an overview of Macaulay inverse
systems. For details, consult [19, Appendix A] and [8, Theorem 21.6]. Let S =
k[y1 , . . . , yn ]DP denote the divided powers algebra in n divided powers variables of
degree −1 over k. We equip S with an R-module structure, called contraction, defined
by extending the following action on monomials, by linearity in both arguments:
                                                  (
                                                     (e −d )     (e −d )
                              (e )                 y1 1 1 · · · yn n n if ei − di ≥ 0 for all i
           xd11 · · · xdnn ◦ y1 1 · · · yn(en ) =
                                                   0                     otherwise .
It is well-known that S = Homk (R, k) is an injective hull of k over R, when considered
                                                      (e )    (e )
as an R-module. We refer to the basis elements y1 1 · · · yn n of S as monomials, noting
                                              e1   e
that they are dual to the monomials x1 · · · xn , and we refer to the elements of S as
                                                    n

polynomials g(y1 , . . . , yn ) in the (divided powers) variables yi .
   If I is a homogeneous ideal of R, then the Macaulay inverse system of I is the graded
R-submodule of S given by
                   I −1 := AnnS (I) = {g ∈ S : f ◦ g = 0 for all f ∈ I}.
Since AnnS (I) ∼= HomR (R/I, S), the inverse system I −1 is isomorphic to the Matlis
dual of R/I. It is thus a consequence of Matlis duality that
                    AnnR (I −1 ) = I      and      (AnnR (W ))−1 = W .
where W is any graded R-submodule of S.

2.2. Narrow and extremely narrow algebras. Let A = R/I be an artinian algebra
quotient of R, with I a homogeneous ideal. Denote by s(A) the top socle degree of
A and by t(I) be the initial degree of I, which is defined as the smallest degree of a
minimal generator of I. Following [15], we say that A is narrow if t(I) ≥ s(A), that is,
the top socle degree of A is at most the initial degree of I.
   Set d = s(A). Let F1 , . . . , Fa ∈ (I −1 )−d and define
                                                                 a
                                 (                                            )
                                                                 X
                 LF1 ,...,Fa := (ℓ1 , ℓ2 , . . . , ℓa ) ∈ R1 a :   ℓi ◦ Fi = 0 .
                                                              i=1
The k-vector space LF1 ,...,Fa is independent, up to isomorphism, of the choice of the
forms F1 , . . . , Fa . When working with properties invariant under isomorphism (for
example, when talking about the dimension of this space), we will also write LW
instead of LF1 ,...,Fa , where W is the vector space spanned by F1 , . . . , Fa . Furthermore,
when W = (I −1 )−d , we also write LA instead of LW .
   Let d ≥ 1. As in [15], we say that A is d-extremely narrow if the following hold:
     (i) s(A) = t(I) = d;
    (ii) There exists a basis F1 , . . . , Fa of (I −1 )−d and x ∈ R1 such that
                                    LF1 ,...,Fa ⊆ x(R0 )a .                             (2.2)

Remark 2.2. Assume the hypotheses of Proposition 2.1. If LF1 ,...,Fa = 0, then the
conclusion that I is generated in degree d, and hence A is d-extremely narrow, also
holds when n < 3. Indeed, since A is narrow, it follows from [15, Lemma 4.2] that

syzygies on a basis of (I −1 )−d and I −1 is generated in degrees −d and −d + 1, we see

2.3. Weak Lefschetz Property. The algebra A is said to have the Weak Lefschetz
                                                         ℓ
Property (abbreviated WLP) if the multiplication Ai−1 −  → Ai by a general linear form
ℓ has maximal rank for all i. More precisely, if we parametrize the elements of R1
by a projective space Pn−1 using their coefficients, then A has WLP if there exists a
                                                  ℓ
nonempty open subset U of Pn−1 such that Ai−1 −   → Ai for all i and all ℓ parametrized
by U . In general, neither homological invariants of artinian rings such as their betti
numbers nor information on their Hilbert functions can be used to determine whether
an algebra satisfies the WLP; see [36, Example 3.4] or [1]. However, in the case of
d-extremely narrow algebras we are able to prove the WLP, and we can also describe
the non-Weak Lefshetz locus.
Proposition 2.3. If A = R/I is d-extremely narrow, then A has the Weak Lefschetz
Property. More precisely, if ℓ ∈ R1 is not a multiple of x, where x ∈ R1 is as in (2.2),
                     ℓ
then the map Ai−1 −
                  → Ai has maximal rank for all i.
Proof. By Proposition 2.1 and the definition of a d-extremely narrow algebra, we know

             3. Orthogonality in rings of symmetric polynomials
   In this section, we keep the notation established in Section 2. We define the rings
of invariants R′ , S ′ , explore choices of bases for the graded components of these rings,
and define the map denoted ⊥ in Eq. (1.4).
3.1. Partitions. A partition of a positive integer d is a tuple of integers λ = (λ1 , . . . , λp )
such that λ1 ≥ λ2 ≥ · · · ≥ λp > 0 and |λ| = λ1 + · · · + λp = d. We denote the fact that
λ is a partition of d by λ ⊢ d. For a partition λ we write #λ for the number of parts,
not to be confused with |λ|, the sum of the parts of λ.
                                                                     λ
   If λ = (λ1 , . . . , λp ) ⊢ d and p ≤ n, we set xλ = xλ1 1 · · · xp p .
                                                                                          λ
   If λ = (λ1 , . . . , λp ) ⊢ d, we say that a monomial m has type λ if m = xλi11 . . . xipp for
some integers i1 , . . . , ip , equivalently, m = σ · xλ for some σ ∈ Sn .
   We utilize the lexicographic order on partitions defined as follows: for partitions
λ ⊢ d and µ ⊢ d we say that λ >Lex µ if the leftmost nonzero entry of the vector λ − µ
is positive.
3.2. Action of the permutation group. We denote by Sn the permutation group
on {1, . . . , n}. We consider the action of Sn on R, respectively S, by
               σf (x1 , . . . , xn ) = f (xσ(1) , . . . , xσ(n) )        for f ∈ R, σ ∈ Sn
                 σg(y1 , . . . , yn ) = g(yσ(1) , . . . , yσ(n) )       for g ∈ S, σ ∈ Sn
As discussed in [15, Lemma 3.2, Appendix A], the action on S is naturally induced
from the action on R, and it satisfies
                                      σ · (f ◦ g) = (σ · f ) ◦ (σ · g)                           (3.1)
for f ∈ R, g ∈ S and σ ∈ Sn . We denote by R′ , respectively S ′ , the subring of
invariants of R, respectively S ′ , under the action of Sn , namely
                            R′ = {f ∈ R | σ · f = f             for all σ ∈ Sn }
                              ′
                            S = {g ∈ S | σ · g = g             for all σ ∈ Sn }
  For each d ≥ 0, we let Pn (d) denote dimk Rd′ . Observe that Pn (d) is the number of
partitions of d with at most n parts. In particular, Pn (d) does not depend on n when
n ≥ d. In this case, we write P (d) instead of Pn (d).
                               GENERAL SYMMETRIC IDEALS                                      11

    When char(k) > n or char k = 0, the Reynolds operator is the algebra retract

              5. Narrow algebras with general invariant socle
   In this section, we use the notation in Section 2 for fixed positive integers n, d, r with
r ≤ Pn (d). We study the parametrization of symmetric ideals in terms of their socle
given by the map β in (1.3).
Definition 5.1. Let 0 ≤ s < Pn (d). We say that a quotient R/I is a narrow algebra
with (s, d)–invariant socle if the inverse system of I has the form I −1 = W + S≥−d+1 ,
where W is a vector subspace of S−d  ′   and dimk (W ) = s.
   We parametrize the space W by its orthogonal complement U ∈ Gr(Pn (d) − s, Rd′ ),
where U ⊥ = W . We say that a general narrow algebra A with (s, d)–invariant socle
satisfies a property (P) if there exists a nonempty set G in Gr(Pn (d) − s, Rd′ ) such that
the property (P) holds for A = R/I, where I = AnnR (U ⊥ + S≥−d+1 ) with U ∈ G.
  The main result of the section, Theorem 5.2, says that, under appropriate as-
sumptions on d, s and n, a general narrow algebra with (s, d)–invariant socle is d-
extremely narrow. For the purpose of later connections, we state the result in terms of
r = Pn (d) − s, where 1 ≤ r ≤ Pn (d).
  Recall that Pn (d) is independent of n when n ≥ d, and we denote it P (d) in this case.
Since the dimension of Rd′ is equal to P (d), we identify the domain of β, Gr(r, Rd′ ),
with Gr(r, kP (d) ) by identifying the basis {mλ }λ⊢d with the standard basis of kPn (d) . An
important aspect of our result is uniformity with respect to the number of variables,
when n ≥ d, as implied by the last statement of Theorem 5.2 below.
Theorem 5.2. Assume n, d, r are positive integers with r ≤ Pn (d), and char k > n or
char k = 0. There exists a nonempty open subset G of Gr(r, Rd′ ) such that if U ∈ G,
then the ideal J = AnnR (U ⊥ + S⩾−d+1 ) and the algebra A = R/J satisfy the following
properties:
   (1) The algebra A is narrow with dimk Jd = dimk Rd − (Pn (d) − r). In particular,
        J = md when r = Pn (d).
   (2) If r < Pn (d), then A is d-extremely narrow, with socle polynomial
   dimk Rd−1 − (Pn (d) − r)n + max{Pn (d) − Pn (d − 1) − r, 0} z d−1 + (Pn (d) − r)z d .
                                                              

     (3) J is generated in degree d.
     (4) The algebra A has the Weak Lefschetz Property. When r < Pn (d), the map
               ℓ
         Ai−1 −→ Ai has maximal rank for all i and all ℓ ∈ R1 such that ℓ is not a
         multiple of x1 + · · · + xn .
Furthermore, when n ≥ d the set G is independent of n, meaning that, when identify-
ing Gr(r, Rd′ ) with Gr(r, kP (d) ), the equations defining G (in Plücker coordinates) have
coefficients that do not depend on n.
   The proof is given at the end of the section, and it is based on the following proposi-
tion, which generalizes [15, Proposition 7.15] and uses notation introduced in Section 4.
Proposition 5.3. Assume the setup of Theorem 5.2 and 1 ≤ r ≤ Pn (d). There exists
a nonempty open subset G of Gr(r, Rd′ ) such that if U ∈ G and W = U ⊥ , then Q(W )
and P(W ) hold and
                       dimk LW = max{Pn (d) − Pn (d − 1) − r, 0} .
                              GENERAL SYMMETRIC IDEALS                                  17

Moreover, when n ≥ d, the set G is independent of the number of variables.
Proof. When d = 1 or n = 1 then, since 1 ≤ r ≤ Pn (d), it follows that r = Pn (d) = 1,
and in this case we set G = Gr(1, R1′ ). In this case W = 0 and dimk LW = 0 as claimed,
and Q(W ), P(W ) hold vacuously. Assume from now on that d ≥ 2 and n ≥ 2.
  For U ∈ Gr(r, Rd′ ), we set W = U ⊥ and we denote
                    C(U ) = dimk L
                                 eW       and      D(U ) = dimk LW .
Let Λ0 be the set of smallest Pn (d) − r partitions of d with respect to the lexicographic
order. Setting
       U0 = ⟨mλ : λ ̸∈ Λ0 ⟩ ⊆ Rd    yields U0 ⊥ = ⟨Mλ : λ ∈ Λ0 ⟩ = WΛ0 ⊆ S−d
                                                                          ′
                                                                             .
We first prove:
Claim 1. There exists a nonempty Zariski open subset G1 of Gr(r, Rd′ ) which is inde-
pendent of n when n ≥ d, such that U0 ∈ G1 and
             C(U ) = max{Pn (d) − Pn (d − 1) − r, 0}             U ∈ G1 .
                                                           for all
  To prove the claim, let U ∈ Gr(r, Rd′ ), let W = U ⊥ and let F = λ⊢d θλ Mλ ∈ S−d
                                                                                 ′ .
                                                                   P

                               (
                                 F ∈ U⊥

              λ⊢d            ν⊢d            λ⊢d
The set of equations above is equivalent to the following system of equations, which is
independent of n when n ≥ d:
                          X
                               cλµ θλ = 0 for all µ ⊢ d − 1.                      (5.2)
                            λ⊢d

   Recall from Lemma 3.2 that cλµ ̸= 0 if and only if λ can be obtained by adding
a box to µ and possibly re-ordering. In particular, this implies that if cλµ ̸= 0 then
λ ≥Lex µ□ , where lex refers to the lexicographic order and µ□ ⊢ d is the partition µ
followed by an additional part equal to 1. Moreover, if µ is the i-th smallest partition
of d − 1 in the lexicographic order then µ□ is the i-th smallest partition of d in the
lexicographic order. Thus, arranging the partitions of d and d − 1 in lexicographic
order from smallest to largest, this implies that the Pn (d − 1) × Pn (d) matrix with
scalar entries cµλ of the system (5.2) is in row echelon form with pivots in every row,
18                                A. SECELEANU AND L. ŞEGA

occupying the first Pn (d − 1) columns. In particular the rank of the matrix cλµ is
                                                                                    

Pn (d − 1).
  Next we turn to the first conditionP in (5.1), namely that F ∈ U ⊥ . Consider a basis for
U consisting of r polynomials ui = λ⊢d ui,λ mλ . Due to (3.5), the condition F ∈ U ⊥
becomes                     X
                               ui,λ θλ = 0 for all 1 ≤ i ≤ r.                        (5.3)
                            λ⊢d
  Upon combining the equations (5.2) and (5.3), we argue next that the corresponding
(Pn (d − 1) + r) × Pn (d) matrix
                                   λ 
                                    cµ
                             AU =
                                   ui,λ µ⊢d−1,i=1,...,r,λ⊢d
attains maximal rank max{Pn (d − 1) + r, Pn (d)}, provided that U is chosen in an
appropriate open set of Gr(r, Rd′ ). First, note that if U = U0 , then the matrix formed
by the last r rows of AU0 , coming from (5.3), is in echelon form, with pivots in the last
r columns. Recalling that the matrix formed by the first Pn (d − 1) rows of AU0 is in
echelon form with pivots in the first Pn (d − 1) columns, we conclude that AU0 has rank
Pn (d − 1) + r provided that Pn (d − 1) + r does not exceed Pn (d), and Pn (d) otherwise.
   The condition that the matrix AU does not have maximal rank is the vanishing of
its maximal minors. The maximal minors of AU can be written      by generalized Laplace
expansion as linear combinations of the maximal minors of ui,λ with coefficients given
by complementary minors of cλµ . That is, the locus where AU fails to have maximal
                                
rank is cut out by linear equations in the Plücker coordinates of U . Therefore, the
complement G1 of the set cut out by these equations is open and U0 ∈ G1 by the
previous considerations. The set G1 does not depend on n when n ≥ d, since the
entries of AU , which determine the complement of G1 , are independent of n.
   Since AU has maximal rank on the set G1 , we conclude that
              C(U ) = Pn (d) − rank AU = max{Pn (d) − Pn (d − 1) − r, 0}
for all U ∈ G1 .
   We now show:
Claim 2. There exists a nonempty open set G2 of Gr(r, Rd′ ), which is independent of n
when n ≥ d, such that Q(U ⊥ ) holds for all U ∈ G2 .
                                                                                   ′ :

  To prove Claim 2, consider the following two conditions on F = λ⊢d θλ Mλ ∈ S−d
                                  (x1 − x2 ) ◦ F = 0   and

                                        F ∈ U⊥ ,

where U has a basis consisting of ui =         λ⊢d ui,λ mλ , with 1 ≤ i ≤ r. For a given
U , the condition Q(U ⊥ ) holds if and only if the equations (5.4) imply F = 0. As
seen above, the condition F ∈ U ⊥ translates as the equations (5.3). Further, upon
writing the expression (x1 − x2 ) ◦ F in terms of the monomial basis of S−d+1 and
equating the coefficients to 0, the condition (x1 −x2 )◦F = 0 translates into dimk S−d+1
linear equations in the variables θλ . We denote by CU the matrix of this system.
Thus, (5.4) translates into a homogeneous system of dimk S−d+1 + r equations in Pn (d)
                              GENERAL SYMMETRIC IDEALS                                    19

indeterminates. Using Lemma 4.8(3) we deduce that Q(W ) holds for W = WΛ0 =
U0 ⊥ , meaning that, when U = U0 , the system (5.4) has only the trivial solution. In
general, for U ∈ Gr(r, Rd′ ), the condition that the system has only the trivial solution
is equivalent to the fact that its matrix has maximal rank. This matrix has the form
                                            
                                          CU
                                  BU =                      .
                                         ui,λ i=1,...,r,λ⊢d
As observed earlier, when U = U0 the matrix formed by the last r rows of BU0 is in
row echelon form, with pivots in the last r columns, and hence there exists a maximal
nonzero minor M0 of BU0 that uses these last r rows. For any U , the condition
that the maximal minor of BU using the same rows and columns as M0 is zero is a
linear equation in the Plücker coordinates of U . The complement G(n) of the set cut
out by this equation is thus open, and contains U0 . We conclude that there exists a
nonempty open set G(n) for which (5.4) implies F = 0 whenever U ∈ G(n). In view
of Lemma 4.8(2), we see that P(U ⊥ ) holds for all U ∈ G(n). The set G(n) depends
on n because the matrix CU depends on n. However, when n ≥ d, we describe next a
nonempty open set that does not depend on n, while satisfying the same properties.
    Assume n ≥ d, and hence Pn (d) = P (d). Since the bijection that takes an r-
dimensional subspace of Rd′ to its (P (d) − r)-dimensional orthogonal complement in
  ′
S−d    induces an isomorphism of algebraic varieties between the respective Grassman-
nians, the set G(d)⊥ = {U ⊥ | U ∈ G(d)} is an open subset of the Grassmannian of
(P (d) − r)-dimensional subspaces of degree −d invariant polynomials in k[y1 , . . . , yd ].
We parametrize G(d) using Plücker coordinates corresponding to the basis {mλ }λ⊢d
and G(d)⊥ using the Plücker coordinates corresponding to the dual basis {Mλ }λ⊢d , cf.
                                                                          −1
(3.1). We use the map δ introduced in Notation 4.7. Since δ(Mλ ) = nd         Mλ , where
the first Mλ is a polynomial in n variables and the second is a polynomial in d variables,
                                             −P (d)+r
δ multiplies each Plücker coordinate by nd            and thus induces the identity map
on tuples of Plücker coordinates viewed as coordinates in projective space.
    Let D denote the preimage of G(d)⊥ under δ. Then D is an open subset of the
Grassmannian Gr(P (d) − r, Sd′ ). While the elements of S−d  ′   depend on n, the set D
does not, as the coefficients of its defining equations are the same as those of the set
G(d)⊥ , which does not depend on n. We set then G2 = D⊥ . If U ∈ G2 , then U ⊥ ∈ D
and hence δ(U ⊥ ) ∈ G(d)⊥ , meaning that (δ(U ⊥ ))⊥ ∈ G(d). By the definition of G(d),
we know that Q(δ(U ⊥ )) holds, and hence Q(U ⊥ ) holds by Lemma 4.8(1). This finishes
the proof of Claim 2.
    It follows from Claim 2 and Lemma 4.8 that P(U ⊥ ) also holds for all U ∈ G2 . Then,
Lemma 4.6 gives that C(U ) = D(U ) for all U ∈ G2 . Using also Claim 1, we conclude
           D(U ) = max{Pn (d) − Pn (d − 1) − r, 0}        for all U ∈ G1 ∩ G2 .
which gives the conclusion of our result.                                                 □
  We now give the proof of the theorem.
Proof of Theorem 5.2. Let G be as in Proposition 5.3.
  Part (1) is a direct consequence of Proposition 2.1, noting that dimk U ⊥ = Pn (d) − r.
This statement holds for any U ∈ Gr(r, Rd′ ), and does not require U ∈ G.
20                                   A. SECELEANU AND L. ŞEGA

   For part (2), let U ∈ G and set A = R/J, where J = AnnR (U ⊥ + S⩾−d+1 ), and

                         dimk LU ⊥ = max{Pn (d) − Pn (d − 1) − r, 0} .                              (5.5)
In view of Remark 4.2, we conclude that (2.2) holds with x = x1 + · · · + xn , hence
A is d-extremely narrow when n ≥ 3 by Proposition 2.1. When n < 3, (5.5) gives
dimk LU ⊥ = 0, and hence A is d-extremely narrow as well, by Remark 2.2.
  Part (3) follows from part (1) and part (2). Part (4) follows from Proposition 2.3
when r < Pn (d), and is clear when r = Pn (d).                                    □

6. Defining equations of a narrow algebra with general invariant socle
   In this section, our goal is to find generators up to symmetry for the symmetric ideal
AnnR (U ⊥ + S⩾−d+1 ), where U is in the open set of Theorem 5.2 and n is sufficiently
large. In Theorem 7.9 we will establish that these ideals are the general symmetric
ideals, thus our results in this section ultimately describe the generators of general
(r, d)-symmetric ideals in sufficiently large number of variables. This is established in
Theorem 6.14 below, whose proof ingredients revise and extend some of the arguments
in [15]. A notable aspect of our results is that the generators do not depend on n, as
long as n is sufficiently large.
   First we recall some terminology introduced in [15].
Definition 6.1. Fix a partition λ = (λ1 , · · · , λs ) of d with s parts, with d ≥ 1.
   If m is a monomial of degree d, then we write type(m) = λ if λ is the unique partition
of d such that m has type λ. We denote by () the empty partition with 0 parts and set
type(1) = ().
   We say that b ∈ R is a λ-binomial if b = m − m′ , with m, m′ distinct monomials of
type λ. For b as above, we set g(b) = gcd(m, m′ ) and we say that b is admissible if g(b)
                               m        m′
is relatively prime with both g(b) and g(b) .
Example 6.2. Let d = 3 and λ = (2, 1). Then the λ-binomials x21 x2 −x21 x3 , x21 x2 −x23 x2 ,
x21 x2 − x23 x4 are all admissible, while the binomial x21 x2 − x22 x3 is not admissible.
Remark 6.3. A λ-binomial is either admissible, or else it can be written as a sum of
admissible λ-binomials. For example, consider the decompositions
                    x21 x2 − x22 x3 = (x21 x2 − x21 x3 ) + (x21 x3 − x22 x3 )
              x31 x22 x3 − x33 x21 x2 = (x31 x22 x3 − x34 x25 x6 ) + (x34 x25 x6 − x33 x21 x2 ) .
In fact, when n is sufficiently large, this decomposition can be done with only two
admissible λ-binomials, as in the second equation above.
Definition 6.4. We say that a partition γ is a subpartition of the partition λ, and
we write γ ⊆ λ, if the multiset of parts of γ is a submultiset of the parts of λ. If
γ ⊆ λ, we describe γ by indicating which parts of λ are present in γ as follows. If
γ = (γ1 , · · · , γt ), then we can choose distinct integers k1 , · · · , kt such that Ψi = λki
for all i with 1 ≤ i ≤ t. Since the choice of such integers is not necessarily unique,
we further require that these indices are chosen in order, starting with k1 and ending
with kt and, whenever a choice is to be made, we choose ki to be the smallest of the
available choices. The indices ki are unique and we set T (λ, γ) := {k1 , . . . , kt }.
                                 GENERAL SYMMETRIC IDEALS                                            21

Example 6.5. If λ = (5, 5, 2, 2, 1), then γ = (5, 5, 2, 1) is a subpartition of λ. There
are two choices for k1 with γ1 = λk1 , namely k1 = 1 or k1 = 2. Since we must choose
the smallest of the choices, we take k1 = 1. The only remaining choice for k2 ̸= k1 with
γ2 = λk2 is k2 = 2. Further, there are two choices for k3 with γ3 = λk3 , namely k3 = 3
or k3 = 4. Our definition dictates k3 = 3. Finally, we see that γ4 = 1 = λ5 , and hence
k4 = 5, and thus T ((5, 5, 2, 2, 1), (5, 5, 2, 1)) = {1, 2, 3, 5}.
Example 6.6. Continuing on Example 6.2 above, notice that the type of g(b) with
b = x21 x2 − x21 x3 , x21 x2 − x23 x2 , respectively, x21 x2 − x23 x4 is γ = (2), (1), respectively
(). These are all subpartitions of λ = (2, 1) not equal to λ, and T (λ, γ) = {1}, {2},
respectively ∅.
Remark 6.7. Let d ≥ 1 and let λ = (λ1 , . . . , λs ) be a partition with s parts. Let b be
a λ-binomial and let γ = type(g(b)). The following statements are then equivalent:
    (1) b is admissible;
    (2) γ ⊊ λ, and there exists a choice of indices with i1 , . . . , is distinct and j1 , . . . , js
        distinct such that b = xλi11 · · · xλiss − xλj11 · · · xλjss and
            iℓ = jℓ   for all ℓ ∈ T       and         {iℓ | ℓ ̸∈ T } ∩ {jℓ | ℓ ̸∈ T } = ∅         (6.1)
        where T = T (λ, γ).
  The following is a modification of the construction in [15, Construction 6.8].

        7. Two parametrizations for general (r, d)-symmetric ideals
   Suppose k is infinite with char(k) = 0 or char(k) > n. Fix positive integers d and
r. The goal of this section is to precisely define the notion of general (r, d)-symmetric
ideals and deduce their main properties in Theorem 7.10.
   Towards this end, recall the map Φ : Gr(r, Rd ) → {symmetric (r, d)-ideals} in-
troduced in (1.1), which parametrizes our ideals of interest in terms of points in a
Grassmannian variety. Then we consider a specific nonempty Zariski open set of this
Grassmannian such that the ideals parametrized by points in that open set are our
general (r, d)-symmetric ideals.

Definition 7.5. Assume n > d and n satisfies (7.2). We say that an ideal I of R is a
general (r, d)-symmetric ideal if I = (V )Sn for some V ∈ O.
   Definition 7.5 provides a parametrization of general (r, d)-symmetric ideals by a
nonempty open set of the Grassmannian Gr(r, Rd ) which justifies the use of the word
“general”. This parametrization was introduced in (1.1) as the map Φ and is recalled
below in (7.6). Our next goal is to establish the equivalence of the parametrization of
general (r, d)-symmetric ideals by Gr(r, Rd ) via Φ to another one by Gr(r, Rd′ ) via the
map Ψ in (1.5) and recalled below in (7.7). The one given by the map Ψ is better,
since, as proven in Theorem 7.9, Ψ|G is bijective.
Notation 7.6. We let SI r,d (R) denote the set of all (r, d)-symmetric ideals of R and
then define:

Lemma 7.7. Assume n > d, r < P (d) and n satisfies (7.2). Then for a general
(r, d)-symmetric ideal I there exists U ∈ G such that I = Ψ(U ).
Proof. By the definition of an general (r, d)-symmetric ideal, I = (V )Sn with V ∈ O.

  Lemma 7.7 shows that general symmetric ideals are in Ψ(G), that is, Φ(O) ⊆ Ψ(G).
Using Theorem 6.14 to lift points in G ⊂ Gr(r, Rd′ ) to points in O ⊂ Gr(r, Rd ) explicitly
we establish the equality of these sets under appropriate conditions in Theorem 7.9.
Remark 7.8. In terms of Notation 7.6 we can reformulate Theorem 6.14 in a manner
which reveals that α and Ψ are mutually inverse when restricted to appropriate subsets
of their domains. With the assumptions of Theorem 6.14, we have
    (1) α(V ) = α(Φ(V )) = U .
    (2) If U ∈ G, then Ψ(U ) = Φ(V ). In particular, α(Ψ(U )) = U .
   In what follows, we denote by Φ|O , Ψ|G , α|O , α|Ψ(G) the restrictions of the maps Φ,
Ψ, α respectively α to the indicated sets. We also make the convention to restrict the
codomains of these maps as indicated in the diagram.
   Recall that diagram (1.4) from the introduction aims to reconcile the two previously
mentioned parametrizations Φ and Ψ of (r, d)-symmetric ideals. Below we show that
this diagram commutes. In view of (7.7) it suffices to show that the upper left triangle
of (1.4) commutes. This appears as (7.9) below.
Theorem 7.9. Suppose k is infinite with char(k) = 0 or char(k) > n and let d, r be
positive integers with r ≤ P (d). Assume n is sufficiently large so that Construction 6.8
can be done. Then Ψ(G) = Φ(O) and the map Φ restricted to O admits the factorization
presented in the commutative diagram below:
                                      Φ|O
                            O                   Φ(O) = Ψ(G)
                                                                                      (7.9)
                                α|O          Ψ|G
                                      G
where α|O is surjective and Ψ|G is bijective, with (Ψ|G )−1 = α|Ψ(G) . Furthermore,
O = Φ−1 (Ψ(G)).
Proof. First we show that if U ∈ G, then Ψ(U ) ∈ Φ(O). Indeed, if U ∈ G, then Re-
mark 7.8 gives that Ψ(U ) = Φ(V ) and α(V ) = U for V as in Theorem 6.14. Further-
more, if J = Ψ(U ), then dimk Jd = dimk Rd −(P (d)−r) by Theorem 5.2. Consequently,
V ∈ O and Ψ(U ) ∈ Φ(O). This shows Ψ(G) ⊆ Φ(O).
   Now, starting with V ∈ O, set U = α(V ) ∈ G. By Lemma 7.7 we conclude that
Φ(V ) = Ψ(U ). This shows that (7.9) is commutative and also that Φ(O) ⊆ Ψ(G).
Since we also proved above the reverse inclusion, we conclude Φ(O) = Ψ(G).
   The map Ψ|G is surjective, given the restriction of the codomain to Ψ(G). Since Ψ
is also injective, it must be bijective. Since Φ|O is surjective, then the commutativity
of the diagram implies α|O is surjective.
   Since Φ(O) = Ψ(G), we have O ⊆ Φ−1 (Ψ(G)). To prove the reverse inclusion, let
V ∈ Φ−1 (Ψ(G)). Then Φ(V ) ∈ Ψ(G), and hence Theorem 5.2 shows that dimk Φ(V ) =
dimk Rd −(P (d)−r) and thus V ∈ e    O. Write Φ(V ) = Ψ(U ) with U ∈ G. By Remark 7.8
                                GENERAL SYMMETRIC IDEALS                                  29

we have that α(Ψ(U )) = U , and hence α(Φ(V )) = U ∈ G. Finally, observe that
α(V ) = α(Φ(V )), and we conclude that α(V ) ∈ G, hence V ∈ α−1 (G) ∩ O
                                                                      e = O. We
                                −1                        −1
have showed thus the inclusion Φ (Ψ(G)) ⊆ O, and hence Φ (Ψ(G)) = O.
  The equality α(Ψ(U )) = U for all U ∈ G and the fact that Ψ|G is bijective also
shows that Ψ|G and α|Ψ(G) are inverses.                                        □

  A consequence of Theorem 7.10 is that general (r, d)-symmetric ideals have minimal
Hilbert function among all (r, d)-symmetric ideals.
Corollary 7.11. Assume the setting of Theorem 7.10. If I is a general (r, d)-symmetric
ideal and J is any (r, d)-symmetric ideal, then
                              HFR/I (i) ≤ HFR/J (i)        for all i
Proof. Since both I and J are generated in degree d and [R/I]d+1 = 0, we only need
to prove the inequality for i = d. The inequality is clear when I = md , so we assume
r < P (d).
   Consider the map ρ : R → R′ , and let J ′ = ρ(J). Then we have an induced surjective
map R/J → R′ /J ′ , giving
           HFR/J (d) ≥ HFR′ /J ′ (d) = P (d) − dimk ([J ′ ]d ) ≥ P (d) − r = HFR/I (d)
where the second inequality uses the inequality dimk ([J ′ ]d ) ≤ r, which is justified by
the fact that J ′ is generated by r elements in degree d.                                □

     We end this section with a discussion of a possible generalization of our results.
Definition 7.12. Let s ≥ 1. For each 1 ≤ i ≤ s consider integers ri ≥ 1 and di such
that 2 ≤ d1 < d2 < · · · < ds . We say that an ideal I is an (r1 , . . . , rs ; d1 , . . . , ds )–
symmetric ideal if I = (V )Sn , where
                                     V = Vd1 ⊕ + · · · ⊕ Vds
with Vdi ∈ Gr(ri , Rdi ).
   With the notation in Definition 7.12, one may wonder if we can extend our results
using a similar notion of general (r1 , . . . , rs ; d1 , . . . , ds )–symmetric ideal, that would
involve a nonempty open set in Gr(r1 , Rd1 ) × · · · × Gr(rs , Rds ). However, it turns
out that such an extension does not produce any additional information, as pointed
out below, since a general (r1 , . . . , rs ; d1 , . . . , ds )-symmetric ideal would be equal to a
general (r1 , d1 )–symmetric ideal.
Remark 7.13. With the notation in Definition 7.12, if Vd1 ∈ O, where O is the open
set of Notation 7.4 with r = r1 and d = d1 , then
                                          I = (Vd1 )Sn .
                                  GENERAL SYMMETRIC IDEALS                                 31

Indeed, the assumption that Vd1 ∈ O gives that (Vd1 )Sn is a general (r1 , d1 )–symmetric
ideal, and thus HFR/(Vd1 )Sn (i) = 0 for i > d1 . This implies that
                           Ii ⊇ [(Vd1 )Sn ]i = mi     for all i > d1
and hence the inclusion must be an inequality. Since we also have Ii = [(Vd1 )Sn ]i when
i = d1 for degree reasons, the two ideals must be equal.

                              8. Symmetric inverse systems
   In this section we further develop the theme that most (r, d)-symmetric ideals I can
be understood by examining their Sn -invariant elements, that is, by considering the
ideal I ′ = I ∩ R′ , where R′ is the ring of invariants of R under the action of Sn . The
main result of this section, Theorem 8.1, shows that the ideal I ′ , although merely a
shadow of I, can be used to recover I by means of Macaulay-Matlis duality.
   In what follows, if W is a subset of S then we denote by R ◦ W the R-submodule
of S generated by W . We observe that the dual pairing ◦ between R and S induces a
dual pairing between R′ and S ′ , that we also denote ◦. If I ′ is an ideal of R′ , then we
denote (I ′ )−1 the R′ -submodule of S ′ given by
                       (I ′ )−1 = {g ∈ S ′ : f ◦ g = 0 for all f ∈ I ′ } .
  If I is a general (r, d)-symmetric ideal we show that the following diagram commutes
                          I                  I −1 = W + S≥−d+1
                              ρ                           ρ                            (8.1)

                          I′               (I ′ )−1 = W + S≥−d+1
                                                           ′     .
                                                                         1 P
The vertical maps ρ are given by the Reynolds operator ρ(f ) = n!           σ∈Sn σ · f while
the horizontal maps arise from Macaulay-Matlis duality with respect to the perfect
pairings between R and S (top) and R′ and S ′ (bottom) respectively. The surprising
aspect of the diagram is that I −1 is obtained from (I ′ )−1 by extension of scalars, that
is, I −1 = R ◦ (I ′ )−1 , whereas it is not the case that I is obtained from I ′ by extension
of scalars.
   Next we establish the circle of ideas pictured in diagram (8.1).
Theorem 8.1. Suppose k is infinite with char(k) = 0 or char(k) > n and let d, r
be positive integers. Assume n is sufficiently large so that Construction 6.8 can be

     9. Asymptotic stability with respect to the number of variables
   In this section, we are concerned with how the properties of interest of general
symmetric ideals change with the number of variables.
   We denote R = k[x1 , . . . , xn , . . .], with k a field, the polynomial ring in countably
many variables and Rn = k[x1 , . . . , xn ]. Unlike in previous sections, the subscripts
utilized so far record the Krull dimension of each ring, not internal degrees. The ring
R is the colimit
               S of the directed system of rings Rn .
   Let S∞ = n≥1 Sn be the group of permutations of N that fix all but finitely many
elements. It acts on R by permuting variables in the natural way, that is,
                        σ · f = f (xσ(1) , xσ(2) , . . .) for any σ ∈ S∞ .
This action induces an action of Sn on Rn for every n ∈ N that coincides with that
considered in the previous sections.
                                GENERAL SYMMETRIC IDEALS                                      33

   An ideal I of R is S∞ -invariant if σ · f ∈ I whenever f ∈ I. If I is a S∞ -invariant
ideal, then the sequence of ideals In = I ∩ Rn are symmetric with respect to the action
of Sn on Rn . Moreover the chain satisfies the property that for m ≤ n, σ ∈ Sn and
f ∈ Im , it follows that σ · f ∈ In . A sequence {In }n∈N of ideals that has this property
is called a S∞ -invariant chain. Conversely, given a S∞ -invariant chain {In }n∈N , the
colimit I = limn∈N In is a S∞ -invariant ideal.
              −→
   As R is Noetherian up to symmetry by [6], any S∞ -invariant ideal can be generated
by finitely many elements f1 , . . . , fr of R, thus has the form

                    I = (f1 , . . . , fr )S∞ = (σ · fi | σ ∈ S∞ , 1 ≤ i ≤ r) .

Setting m to be the largest index of a variable in the union of the supports of f1 , . . . , fr
gives that I is the colimit of the chain Im ⊆ Im+1 ⊆ · · · In ⊆ · · · , where In =
(f1 , . . . , fr )Sn for each n ≥ m.
   We apply the results from our previous sections to study chains of S∞ -invariant
ideals as above where f1 , . . . , fr are general forms of degree d. Since n is no longer
fixed, an adjustment of our previously used notation is needed.

Notation 9.1. For each n ≥ d, we identify the k-vector spaces [Rn′ ]d with kP (d) by
identifying a basis of [Rn′ ]d with the standard basis of kP (d) . This leads to an identifi-
cation of Gr(r, [Rn′ ]d ) with Gr(r, kP (d) ) for all n ≥ d. In Theorem 5.2, we established
existence of a nonempty open subset G of the Grassmannian Gr(r, [Rn′ ]d ) with certain
properties, and we made the point that this set is independent of n when n ≥ d, in
the sense that the defining equations (in Plücker coordinates) of its complement have
coefficients that do not depend on n. Via the identifications discussed above, we may
think of this set as a nonempty open subset G of Gr(r, kP (d) ) whenever n ≥ d. While
this set G is independent of n, the set O and the maps α, Φ, Ψ defined in (7.3), (7.6),
and (7.7) depend on n, and in this section we denote them On , αn , Φn and Ψn to
indicate this dependence.
   Recall that SI r,d (Rn ) denotes the set of symmetric (r, d) ideals in the ring Rn . To
simplify notation, since r and d are fixed, we write SI(Rn ) instead of SI r,d (Rn ). We
further let SI g (Rn ) denote the set of general (r, d)-symmetric ideals in Rn .
   Let n, m be integers with n ≤ m. We define canonical maps

  πn,m : Gr(r, [Rn ]d ) → Gr(r, [Rm ]d )         πn,m (V ) := V
  ηn,m : SI(Rn ) → SI(Rm )                       ηn,m (I) := ISm = {σ · f : σ ∈ Sm , f ∈ I}

   In Theorem 7.9 we established a commutative diagram, in which the maps involved
are restrictions of the maps α, Ψ, Φ. In Theorem 9.2 below, which compares the
commutative diagrams given in (7.9) for different values of n, the maps involved are
also restrictions, but we decided to omit the restriction symbols from the diagram (i.e.
we write αn instead of αn |On ), in order to avoid notation overload.

   In the following theorem we prove that our family of general (r, d)-symmetric ideals
is asymptotically constant upon increasing the number of variables in a sense made
precise by the bijection ηn,m below.
34                               A. SECELEANU AND L. ŞEGA

Theorem 9.2. Suppose k is a field with char(k) = 0 and let d, r be positive integers
with r ≤ P (d). If m is sufficiently large to allow for Construction 6.8, then for all
n ≥ m the following hold:
   (1) The map ηm,n restricts to a bijection ηm,n : SI g (Rm ) → SI g (Rn ).
   (2) πm,n (Om ) ⊆ On .
   (3) There is a commutative diagram, in which all arrows in the rightmost triangle
       are bijections.
                                              Φn
              On                                                                    SI g (Rn )

                                      αm      Ψm

In particular, if I is a general (r, d)-symmetric ideal of Rm , then ISn is a general
(r, d)-symmetric ideal of Rn for all n ≥ m.

                        Ψn (U ) = ηm,n Ψm (U )              for all U ∈ G                        (9.2)

and Ψn : G → SI g (Rn ) are bijective by Theorem 7.9, we conclude that the map
ηm,n : SI g (Rm ) → SI g (Rn ) is bijective as well.
   It can be easily checked from the definitions that
             ηm,n Φm (V ) = Φn πm,n (V )            and           αn πm,n (V ) = αm (V )         (9.3)
for all V ∈ Gr(r, [Rm ]d ). We want to now show πm,n (Om ) ⊆ On . Recall that by

   The commutativity of the left triangle and of the trapezoid on top then follows from

  Let {In }n≥0 be a S∞ -invariant chain of homogeneous ideals with colimit I. Its
equivariant Hilbert series is defined in [29] as a bivariate generating series encoding all
the Hilbert series of the quotient rings Rn /In simultaneously
                            X                   XX
                HI (s, t) =     HRn /In (t)sn =         dimk [Rn /In ]u tu sn .       (9.4)
                            n≥0                     n≥0 u≥0

  We summarize the key features that the numerical invariants of S∞ -invariant chains
I are known to possess:
(1) The equivariant Hilbert series HI (s, t) is a rational function of the form
                                                     g(s, t)
                      HI (s, t) =              Qb
                                    (1 − t)a     i=1 ((1 − t)
                                                                ai − sf (t))
                                                                       i
    for some integers a, b, ai and some polynomials g ∈ Z[s, t], fi ∈ Z[t]; see [29,
    Proposition 7.2].
(2) The Krull dimension and the height of In are eventually linear functions of n: by
    [27, Teorem 5.14] and [22, Theorem 7.10] there exist A, B, A′ , B ′ ∈ Z such that
             dim(Rn /In ) = An + B and ht(In ) = A′ n + B ′ for all n ≫ 0.
(3) The multiplicity grows eventually exponentially by [28]. More precisely, there are
    M, L ∈ Z and Q ∈ Q such that
                                      e(Rn /In )
                                     lim         = Q.
                                 n→∞ M n nL
(4) The regularity of In is bounded by a linear function of n: by [23, Corollaries 4.6,
    4.7] there exist C, D ∈ Z such that
                             reg(In ) ≤ Cn + D for all n ≫ 0.                         (9.5)
(5) For any i ≥ 0, the i-th column of the Betti table of In has a stable shape whenever
    n ≫ 0. More precisely, there exist integers j0 < · · · < jt depending on i and I
    such that for n ≫ 0
                       βi,j (In ) ̸= 0 if and only if j ∈ {j0 , . . . , jt }.
    For more precise statements regarding stabilization of Betti numbers see [30].
  It is conjectured in [23, Conjecture 1.1] that equality holds in (9.5) for appropri-
ate values of C, D and that a similar property is true for projective dimension [22,
Conjecture 1.1], namely that there exist E, F ∈ Z so that
                             pd(In ) ≤ En + F for all n ≫ 0.                          (9.6)
Both conjectures are known to hold true when the quotients Rn /In are artinian and
also for S∞ -invariant chains of monomial ideals [25], [32].
   We may also define the (i, j)-equivariant betti series of I by

for all i, j, and the equivariant bigraded Poincaré series of I by
                                            X

                                           i≥0,j≥0

While it seems that this question has not been explicitly stated so far, it is natural to
ask whether βi,j (I, s) is a rational function of s, and, furthermore, if PI (s, t, u) is a
rational function in s, t, u.
   In the following result we describe the features of S∞ -invariant chains of general
(r, d)-symmetric ideals. A surprising outcome is that for these chains the algebraic
invariants exhibit slower growth than for arbitrary S∞ –invariant chains. For example,
while the multiplicity of arbitrary S∞ -invariant chains grows exponentially, for general
chains it grows polynomially.

Theorem 9.3. Suppose k is a field with char(k) = 0 and let d, r be positive integers
with r ≤ P (d). Assume m is sufficiently large to allow for Construction 6.8. Let I be
a general (r, d)-symmetric ideal of Rm , and consider the S∞ -invariant chain {In }n∈N
with In = (I)Sn and colimit I. Using the notation

                           ℓ = max{P (d) − P (d − 1) − r, 0}
                           a = P (d) − r,

the following hold:
     (1) dim(Rn /In ) = 0 and ht(In ) = n for all n ≥ m, i.e, the rings Rn /In are artinian.
     (2) pdRn (Rn /In ) = n for all n ≥ m
     (3) regRn (Rn /In ) = d for all n ≥ m
     (4) the i-th betti numbers of Rn /In are polynomials in n of degree d + i for all
         0 ≤ i ≤ n − 1, while the n-th betti number of Rn /In is a linear function of n.
     (5) The equivariant Hilbert series in its reduced form is
                                 hP                     i
                                     d−1        j td−1−j + a(1 − s)d−1 td
                               s     j=0 (1 − s)

     (6) The multiplicity of Rn /In grows polynomially as a function of n with

                                       e(Rn /In )      1
                                 lim              =          .
                                n→∞      nd−1       (d − 1)!

    (7) The equivariant betti number βi,j (I, s) is a rational function of s for all i, j,
         and the equivariant bigraded Poincaré series PI (s, t, u) is a rational function of
         s, t, u. More precisely,
